No Hack Required: Two Outages, One Week, and the AI Agent Problem Nobody Is Governing

Microsoft went dark across 74 countries. The FAA grounded every US flight. Neither was a cyberattack. In the same week, Google confirmed an AI agent running an attack with no human involved.

Lisa Warren · Neural Horizons AI · 18 November 2026 · 7 min read

On this pageThe week it blinkedThe theoriesAgents attackAgents spendThe weak linkSources

Two of the world's most relied-on systems failed within 24 hours. Neither was a hack. Both showed how little visibility most organisations have into what they depend on. Now add AI agents that can act on their own.

Not everything this week was an outage

Some of it was a real attack, and it came through a supplier. On 16 November an attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation and planted malicious code in scripts that customers' sites load from the service. Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organisations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received it, according to Report URI. Norway's Equinor confirmed an ongoing attack on its IT systems on 17 November, with no impact on production reported. Visa said an incident involved a third-party provider in Asia Pacific, not its own systems, after a ransomware group listed it and JPMorgan on a leak site. Both banks dispute the claims, and the evidence published so far does not establish a breach of either. Three different stories, one lesson: the exposure sits in the dependencies you did not map.

Updated, 18 November (evening)

The pattern has continued since this was published. On 16 November, Chase and other US banks reported outages. Chase attributed it to a software bug in on-premise hardware and said there was no evidence it was cyber-related. On 17 November, Apple said an internal update caused outages across iCloud, Apple Pay and the App Store, and ruled out a cyberattack. Charles Schwab users also reported an app outage.

The NSA's classified internal network also went down on 17 November. The agency cited scheduled maintenance, and the Director of National Intelligence said a security patch caused some systems not to come back up as expected. That is five major disruptions in six days, and every official explanation so far is non-cyber. Some people online are convinced it is one coordinated attack. We found no evidence for that.

The explanation now taking shape is patching. The DNI tied the NSA outage to a patch for PHP flaws found last month. Reports citing anonymous sources say bank executives and NSA officials told Congress that the rush to fix vulnerabilities found by AI overwhelmed systems. Nobody on the record says AI caused the outages. The point is that AI is finding flaws faster than organisations can safely fix them. On 17 November a Java flaw nicknamed Java4Shell was disclosed, found by researchers using AI in about an hour. CISA urged immediate patching, and we saw no evidence of attacks using it at the time of writing.

Two lessons. First, one analysis of the Apple outage noted that every Apple service hangs off the same Apple ID, so a single sign-in failure cascaded across the ecosystem. That is the dependency problem in one sentence. Second, expect scams. A cybersecurity expert has warned of fraud after the bank outage, so treat any "your account is locked" message as suspect and go to the app directly.

⬡ 01 — The week the systems blinked

On Thursday 12 November, Microsoft began investigating Exchange Online problems in the Americas. Within hours it widened the scope to Microsoft 365 users in any region. Outlook, Teams, OneDrive and Copilot were hit. Reports counted 74 countries and territories, with services still unstable into 13 November.

Microsoft said from the start that it had no indication of malicious activity. Its preliminary post-incident report, shared on 16 November, blames a months-old software defect in a fix for its networking gateway servers. A traffic surge after a Teams failover and reduced server capacity combined with it. The disruption ran for close to 24 hours. One tally counts this as at least the fifth major Microsoft 365 outage of 2026.

The next day, Friday 13 November, at about 3:30 p.m. Eastern, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop. It lasted more than four hours. Fox Weather called it the longest nationwide US airspace ground stop since 9/11. Thousands of flights were cancelled. The FAA cited a technical problem and telecommunications outages. DHS blamed an outdated air traffic control system. CNN reported that early indications pointed away from a cyberattack. The administration later attributed the stoppage to newly installed routers that flooded the FAA's telecommunications system, and the Homeland Security Secretary said he was 98% certain it was not a cyberattack.

What is established

Both disruptions were real and large. Not established: any attacker, any link between the two events, or any AI-agent cause. Anyone telling you otherwise is guessing.

⬡ 02 — Why the theories arrive before the explanations

When critical systems fail and nobody can say why, the explanations show up anyway. Some are plausible. Many are not. They spread because the failure was visible and the cause was not.

That gap is the real story. Most leaders cannot see inside the systems their business runs on. They cannot say what depends on what, who can change it, or what breaks when one piece stops.

“You do not need a villain for the lights to go out. You only need a dependency nobody mapped. The villain is the next problem.”

Lisa Warren, Founder & CEO, Neural Horizons AI

⬡ 03 — Now add an agent that does not blink

On 16 November, Google's Threat Intelligence Group published its Q4 2026 AI threat tracker. It documents what it describes as a first: a suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop. The exploits were then run automatically and used to steal data from victim organisations.

Researchers found a multi-agent framework on an exposed staging server. It compared application code before and after security updates, identified likely weaknesses, built exploits and ran them on its own.

Google also documents other actors, including financially motivated criminals and espionage groups with suspected China links, using autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks for multi-stage intrusions. Its judgement is that this is highly likely to continue, because the barrier to entry is low.

That is a different category of risk from an outage. An outage is a failure nobody chose. This is a capability someone chose, and it scales.

⬡ 04 — Agents are already spending, booking and moving money

The same week showed how quickly agents are being handed real authority.

  • Banking: Fed Governor Michael Barr warned in remarks prepared for a conference in Milan that autonomous agents could speed up bank runs by shifting deposits automatically in response to market signals. He noted that major banks are already detecting AI agents attempting unauthorised actions in retail accounts.
  • Payments: OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Wallet, which lets AI agents complete purchases on a user's behalf.
  • Pushback: United moved against unauthorised AI booking agents, a sign that businesses are starting to fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying.
  • Permissions: Sierra's Poppy 1.0 introduces a protocol that tells personal agents which actions a business permits.

Agents are buying, booking and moving money. Some are acting for you. Some are acting against you. In many organisations, nobody has written down which is which.

⬡ 05 — The weak link is authorisation

Resilience and AI governance are the same question asked two ways: what is allowed to act in our business, and what happens when it fails or is abused?

Before you add another agent, a leadership team should be able to answer five questions quickly and agree on the answers:

  • What depends on what? Which single system, supplier or process would stop revenue if it went down tomorrow?
  • Who can an agent act as? What can each agent access, spend or change, and who approved it?
  • Where does a human sign off? Which actions require approval, and which run unattended?
  • How would we know? Could we detect an agent, ours or someone else's, doing something it should not?
  • Can we stop it? Who has the authority and the ability to switch it off, and how fast?
The business lesson

You cannot govern what you cannot see. Most AI risk starts as an ordinary operational gap between departments, long before it becomes a headline.

This is what the AI Weak-Link Diagnostic is built for. It is a fixed-fee, two-week diagnosis for CEOs, CFOs and COOs in the UAE and GCC. It shows where your business is disconnected, where value is leaking between departments, which AI use cases are safe to start, and what to fix first. It ends in a board readout. It is personally led by me. It is not a penetration test or a cyber audit. It is the operational clarity that has to come first.

Takeaways

  • → Two outages in 24 hours needed no attacker. Unmapped dependency is risk on its own.
  • → Google has documented an AI agent running an attack end to end. Expect more.
  • → Agents are gaining authority to spend and move money faster than most firms are writing rules for them.
  • → The fix starts with visibility: what depends on what, and who authorised what.

If an AI agent started acting in your business tomorrow, would you know what it could touch, who approved it, and how to stop it?
